claim: Cholesterol synthesis requires eleven oxygen molecules per molecule of product.
source: Most cellular cholesterol arises from an energetically expensive biosynthetic pathway requiring eleven oxygen molecules and over one hundred ATP equivalents per molecule of product (Brown et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2021

claim: Cholesterol synthesis requires over one hundred ATP equivalents per molecule of product.
source: Most cellular cholesterol arises from an energetically expensive biosynthetic pathway requiring eleven oxygen molecules and over one hundred ATP equivalents per molecule of product (Brown et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2021

claim: Many intermediates of the cholesterol synthesis pathway are toxic in excess.
source: Furthermore, many intermediates of this pathway are toxic in excess (Porter and Herman, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Porter and Herman, 2011

claim: Squalene monooxygenase catalyzes the rate-limiting conversion of squalene to monooxidosqualene in the committed cholesterol synthesis pathway.
source: Squalene monooxygenase (SM, also known as squalene epoxidase or SQLE, EC:1.14.14.17) catalyzes the rate-limiting conversion of squalene to monooxidosqualene in the committed cholesterol synthesis pathway (Gill et al., 2011; Chua et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gill et al., 2011 and Chua et al., 2020

claim: The SM-catalyzed reaction is the first in the cholesterol synthesis pathway to require molecular oxygen.
source: This reaction is the first in the pathway to require molecular oxygen, with the introduced epoxide group ultimately forming the signature C3-hydroxyl group of cholesterol.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript text

claim: SM can act a second time on monooxidosqualene to produce dioxidosqualene, the precursor of 24(S),25-epoxycholesterol.
source: SM can also act a second time on monooxidosqualene to produce dioxidosqualene, the precursor of the potent regulatory oxysterol 24(S),25-epoxycholesterol (Bai et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bai et al., 1992

claim: SM is subject to transcriptional regulation via sterol regulatory element-binding proteins.
source: As a flux-controlling enzyme, SM is subject to metabolic regulation at both the transcriptional level via sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (Horton et al., 2003) and the post-translational level via ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation (Gill et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horton et al., 2003

claim: SM is subject to post-translational regulation via ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
source: As a flux-controlling enzyme, SM is subject to metabolic regulation at both the transcriptional level via sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (Horton et al., 2003) and the post-translational level via ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation (Gill et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gill et al., 2011

claim: The N-terminal regulatory domain of SM (SM-N100) senses lipid levels in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane.
source: The latter is mediated by the N-terminal regulatory domain of SM (SM-N100), which senses lipid levels in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane and accelerates or attenuates SM degradation in response to excess cholesterol or squalene, respectively (Chua et al., 2017; Yoshioka et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chua et al., 2017 and Yoshioka et al., 2020

claim: SM-N100 accelerates SM degradation in response to excess cholesterol.
source: The latter is mediated by the N-terminal regulatory domain of SM (SM-N100), which senses lipid levels in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane and accelerates or attenuates SM degradation in response to excess cholesterol or squalene, respectively (Chua et al., 2017; Yoshioka et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chua et al., 2017 and Yoshioka et al., 2020

claim: SM-N100 attenuates SM degradation in response to excess squalene.
source: The latter is mediated by the N-terminal regulatory domain of SM (SM-N100), which senses lipid levels in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane and accelerates or attenuates SM degradation in response to excess cholesterol or squalene, respectively (Chua et al., 2017; Yoshioka et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chua et al., 2017 and Yoshioka et al., 2020

claim: Incomplete proteolysis of SM produces a truncated form (trunSM) that lacks a large portion of the SM-N100 domain but retains the full catalytic domain.
source: SM is typically fully degraded by the proteasome; however, incomplete proteolysis produces a truncated form of SM (trunSM) that lacks a large portion of the lipid-sensing SM-N100 domain but retains the full catalytic domain (Coates et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coates et al., 2021

claim: trunSM is cholesterol-resistant and constitutively active.
source: This renders trunSM cholesterol-resistant and therefore constitutively active.
evidence: Stated as fact following description of trunSM structure

claim: Truncation of SM is induced by the SM inhibitor NB-598.
source: Although truncation is induced by the SM inhibitor NB-598, human cell lines express similar levels of full-length and truncated SM (Coates et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coates et al., 2021

claim: Human cell lines express similar levels of full-length and truncated SM.
source: Although truncation is induced by the SM inhibitor NB-598, human cell lines express similar levels of full-length and truncated SM (Coates et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coates et al., 2021

claim: Overexpression of SQLE is associated with greater invasiveness and lethality in breast cancer.
source: Overexpression of the SM gene SQLE is associated with greater invasiveness and lethality in breast (Brown et al., 2016), prostate (Stopsack et al., 2016; Pudova et al., 2020), and pancreatic cancers (Bai et al., 2021), amongst others.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2016

claim: Overexpression of SQLE is associated with greater invasiveness and lethality in prostate cancer.
source: Overexpression of the SM gene SQLE is associated with greater invasiveness and lethality in breast (Brown et al., 2016), prostate (Stopsack et al., 2016; Pudova et al., 2020), and pancreatic cancers (Bai et al., 2021), amongst others.
evidence: Supported by citations to Stopsack et al., 2016 and Pudova et al., 2020

claim: Overexpression of SQLE is associated with greater invasiveness and lethality in pancreatic cancer.
source: Overexpression of the SM gene SQLE is associated with greater invasiveness and lethality in breast (Brown et al., 2016), prostate (Stopsack et al., 2016; Pudova et al., 2020), and pancreatic cancers (Bai et al., 2021), amongst others.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bai et al., 2021

claim: Aberrant SM protein expression is implicated in colorectal cancer progression.
source: At the protein level, aberrant SM expression is implicated in colorectal cancer progression (He et al., 2021; Jun et al., 2021) and the development of both nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma (Liu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to He et al., 2021 and Jun et al., 2021

claim: Aberrant SM protein expression is implicated in the development of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.
source: At the protein level, aberrant SM expression is implicated in colorectal cancer progression (He et al., 2021; Jun et al., 2021) and the development of both nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma (Liu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2021 and Liu et al., 2018

claim: Aberrant SM protein expression is implicated in the development of hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: At the protein level, aberrant SM expression is implicated in colorectal cancer progression (He et al., 2021; Jun et al., 2021) and the development of both nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and hepatocellular carcinoma (Liu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2021 and Liu et al., 2018

claim: Hypoxia is common in the poorly vascularized cores of solid tumors.
source: Given its key role in oxygen-dependent cholesterol synthesis, SM may be particularly critical for cancer cell survival during hypoxia, which is common in the poorly vascularized cores of solid tumors and often associated with poor prognosis (Rankin and Giaccia, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rankin and Giaccia, 2016

claim: Hypoxia in solid tumors is often associated with poor prognosis.
source: Given its key role in oxygen-dependent cholesterol synthesis, SM may be particularly critical for cancer cell survival during hypoxia, which is common in the poorly vascularized cores of solid tumors and often associated with poor prognosis (Rankin and Giaccia, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rankin and Giaccia, 2016

claim: SM inhibition sensitizes breast cancer cells to hypoxia-induced cell death.
source: In support of this idea, SM inhibition sensitizes breast and colorectal cancer cells to hypoxia-induced cell death (Haider et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haider et al., 2016

claim: SM inhibition sensitizes colorectal cancer cells to hypoxia-induced cell death.
source: In support of this idea, SM inhibition sensitizes breast and colorectal cancer cells to hypoxia-induced cell death (Haider et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haider et al., 2016

claim: Hypoxic cells tend to accumulate cholesterol.
source: Although hypoxic cells tend to accumulate cholesterol, there are conflicting reports on changes in biosynthetic flux (Mukodani et al., 1990; Parathath et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mukodani et al., 1990, Parathath et al., 2011, and Wu et al., 2020

claim: Hypoxia affects HMGCR, an early pathway enzyme in cholesterol synthesis.
source: Furthermore, with the notable exception of the early pathway enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase (HMGCR) (Nguyen et al., 2007), the effects of hypoxia on individual biosynthetic enzymes are unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nguyen et al., 2007

claim: Hypoxic conditions induce SM truncation in a variety of cell lines.
source: Here, we show hypoxic conditions induce SM truncation in a variety of cell lines through a combination of accelerated proteasomal degradation and inhibition of its complete proteolysis.
evidence: Stated as a main finding in the abstract

claim: Hypoxia-induced SM truncation occurs through accelerated proteasomal degradation.
source: Here, we show hypoxic conditions induce SM truncation in a variety of cell lines through a combination of accelerated proteasomal degradation and inhibition of its complete proteolysis.
evidence: Stated as a main finding in the abstract

claim: Hypoxia-induced SM truncation occurs through inhibition of complete proteolysis of SM.
source: Here, we show hypoxic conditions induce SM truncation in a variety of cell lines through a combination of accelerated proteasomal degradation and inhibition of its complete proteolysis.
evidence: Stated as a main finding in the abstract

claim: Hypoxia stabilizes the E3 ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6.
source: This occurs due to the accumulation of both MARCHF6, the major E3 ubiquitin ligase for SM, and squalene, which impedes SM degradation through a mechanism involving the SM-N100 regulatory domain.
evidence: Stated as a main finding in the abstract

claim: MARCHF6 is the major E3 ubiquitin ligase for SM.
source: This occurs due to the accumulation of both MARCHF6, the major E3 ubiquitin ligase for SM, and squalene, which impedes SM degradation through a mechanism involving the SM-N100 regulatory domain.
evidence: Stated as fact in the abstract

claim: Squalene accumulates during hypoxia.
source: This occurs due to the accumulation of both MARCHF6, the major E3 ubiquitin ligase for SM, and squalene, which impedes SM degradation through a mechanism involving the SM-N100 regulatory domain.
evidence: Stated as a main finding in the abstract

claim: Squalene impedes SM degradation through a mechanism involving the SM-N100 regulatory domain.
source: This occurs due to the accumulation of both MARCHF6, the major E3 ubiquitin ligase for SM, and squalene, which impedes SM degradation through a mechanism involving the SM-N100 regulatory domain.
evidence: Stated as a main finding in the abstract

claim: SM truncation preserves SM activity during hypoxia.
source: Taken together, our findings point towards a role for the constitutively active trunSM in adaptations to hypoxic conditions and suggest it may contribute to the oncogenic impacts of SM activity.
evidence: Stated as a main conclusion in the abstract

claim: Incubation of HEK293T cells under hypoxic conditions (1% O2) stabilized HIF1α.
source: Incubation of HEK293T cells under hypoxic conditions (1% O2) stabilized hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF1α; Figure 1B) and upregulated its target genes VEGF and CA9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), confirming the induction of a hypoxic response.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Hypoxia upregulated HIF1α target genes VEGF and CA9 in HEK293T cells.
source: Incubation of HEK293T cells under hypoxic conditions (1% O2) stabilized hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF1α; Figure 1B) and upregulated its target genes VEGF and CA9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), confirming the induction of a hypoxic response.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Hypoxia caused the disappearance of full-length SM in HEK293T cells.
source: We also noted a striking increase in SM truncation caused by the disappearance of full-length SM and a four-fold accumulation of trunSM (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Hypoxia caused a four-fold accumulation of trunSM in HEK293T cells.
source: We also noted a striking increase in SM truncation caused by the disappearance of full-length SM and a four-fold accumulation of trunSM (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Hypoxia led to trunSM becoming the predominant SM variant.
source: This led to trunSM becoming the predominant SM variant, as indicated by the elevated trunSM:SM ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: Hypoxia-induced truncation of SM increased over time.
source: Hypoxia-induced truncation of SM increased over time (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and according to the magnitude of oxygen deprivation (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), with the net result of increased total enzyme levels (expressed as the sum of full-length SM and trunSM levels; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: Hypoxia-induced truncation of SM increased according to the magnitude of oxygen deprivation.
source: Hypoxia-induced truncation of SM increased over time (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and according to the magnitude of oxygen deprivation (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), with the net result of increased total enzyme levels (expressed as the sum of full-length SM and trunSM levels; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D

claim: Hypoxia resulted in increased total SM enzyme levels.
source: Hypoxia-induced truncation of SM increased over time (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and according to the magnitude of oxygen deprivation (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), with the net result of increased total enzyme levels (expressed as the sum of full-length SM and trunSM levels; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: trunSM accumulation was greater under severely hypoxic conditions (0.5–2% O2) than under physoxic conditions (3–7.5% O2).
source: Importantly, trunSM accumulation was greater under the severely hypoxic conditions characteristic of solid tumors (0.5–2% O2) than the 'physoxic' conditions experienced by normal human tissues in situ (3–7.5% O2) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D; McKeown, 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, with citation to McKeown, 2014 for oxygen level definitions

claim: Severely hypoxic conditions (0.5–2% O2) are characteristic of solid tumors.
source: Importantly, trunSM accumulation was greater under the severely hypoxic conditions characteristic of solid tumors (0.5–2% O2) than the 'physoxic' conditions experienced by normal human tissues in situ (3–7.5% O2) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D; McKeown, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to McKeown, 2014

claim: Physoxic conditions (3–7.5% O2) are experienced by normal human tissues in situ.
source: Importantly, trunSM accumulation was greater under the severely hypoxic conditions characteristic of solid tumors (0.5–2% O2) than the 'physoxic' conditions experienced by normal human tissues in situ (3–7.5% O2) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D; McKeown, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to McKeown, 2014

claim: Increased SM truncation is a feature of pathophysiological hypoxia.
source: This suggested that increased SM truncation is a feature of pathophysiological hypoxia.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that truncation is greater under tumor-like hypoxic conditions

claim: SM truncation is increased at higher cell densities.
source: We also noted our experiments, which for technical reasons used a variety of cell seeding densities, showed variation in the normoxic trunSM:SM ratio. Indeed, we confirmed SM truncation is increased at higher cell densities and accompanied by slight stabilization of HIF1α (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), consistent with other reports (Sheta et al., 2001; Dayan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and citations to Sheta et al., 2001 and Dayan et al., 2009

claim: Higher cell densities are accompanied by slight stabilization of HIF1α.
source: Indeed, we confirmed SM truncation is increased at higher cell densities and accompanied by slight stabilization of HIF1α (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), consistent with other reports (Sheta et al., 2001; Dayan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and citations to Sheta et al., 2001 and Dayan et al., 2009

claim: Hypoxia-induced accumulation of trunSM was generalizable to all cell lines tested.
source: We also surveyed SM levels in a panel of cell lines and found hypoxia-induced accumulation of trunSM was generalizable to all, although full-length SM levels did not decline in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F

claim: Full-length SM levels did not decline in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells during hypoxia.
source: We also surveyed SM levels in a panel of cell lines and found hypoxia-induced accumulation of trunSM was generalizable to all, although full-length SM levels did not decline in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F

claim: Knockdown of HIF1A and HIF2A expression had no effect on the magnitude of hypoxia-induced SM truncation in HEK293T cells.
source: However, knockdown of HIF1A and HIF2A expression to a level sufficient to reduce target gene activation (Sena et al., 2014) had no effect on the magnitude of hypoxia-induced SM truncation in HEK293T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B and citation to Sena et al., 2014

claim: HIF1α and HIF2α are not involved in hypoxia-induced SM truncation.
source: This ruled out the involvement of HIF1α, HIF2α and their target genes in this phenomenon.
evidence: Inferred from the knockdown experiment results

claim: SM is truncated via partial proteasomal degradation.
source: As SM is truncated via partial proteasomal degradation (Coates et al., 2021), we reasoned that hypoxia promotes this through a two-step mechanism: (1) targeting of full-length SM to the proteasome, and (2) inhibition of its complete proteolysis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Coates et al., 2021

claim: SQLE transcripts were downregulated in hypoxic HEK293T cells.
source: SQLE transcripts were downregulated in hypoxic HEK293T cells, as were transcripts encoding the upstream cholesterol synthesis enzyme HMGCR (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: HMGCR transcripts were downregulated in hypoxic HEK293T cells.
source: SQLE transcripts were downregulated in hypoxic HEK293T cells, as were transcripts encoding the upstream cholesterol synthesis enzyme HMGCR (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Downregulation of SQLE transcripts was not observed in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Downregulation of SQLE transcripts was not observed in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), accounting for the unchanged full-length SM levels in this cell line.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The reduction in SQLE and HMGCR transcripts in HEK293T cells likely reflected a broad transcriptional suppression of cholesterol synthesis during hypoxia.
source: Although the reduction in SQLE and HMGCR transcripts in HEK293T cells likely reflected a broad transcriptional suppression of cholesterol synthesis during hypoxia, as reported previously (Dolt et al., 2007; Cao et al., 2014), the magnitude of SQLE downregulation was unlikely to fully explain the large reduction in SM protein levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dolt et al., 2007 and Cao et al., 2014

claim: The magnitude of SQLE downregulation was unlikely to fully explain the large reduction in SM protein levels during hypoxia.
source: Although the reduction in SQLE and HMGCR transcripts in HEK293T cells likely reflected a broad transcriptional suppression of cholesterol synthesis during hypoxia, as reported previously (Dolt et al., 2007; Cao et al., 2014), the magnitude of SQLE downregulation was unlikely to fully explain the large reduction in SM protein levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of transcript and protein level changes

claim: Levels of constitutively expressed SM construct ([HA]3-SM-V5) were markedly reduced during extended hypoxic incubations with no associated change in mRNA levels.
source: Moreover, levels of a constitutively expressed SM construct ([HA]3-SM-V5) were markedly reduced during extended hypoxic incubations with no associated change in mRNA levels (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Hypoxia reduces the levels of full-length SM through both transcriptional downregulation and accelerated post-translational degradation.
source: We concluded that hypoxia reduces the levels of full-length SM through both transcriptional downregulation and accelerated post-translational degradation.
evidence: Concluded from the experimental observations of transcript and protein changes

claim: Levels of SM-N100-GFP-V5 were reduced by hypoxic conditions.
source: Like full-length SM, levels of SM-N100-GFP-V5 were reduced by hypoxic conditions (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Proteasomal inhibition using MG132 increased the levels of SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5.
source: Proteasomal inhibition using MG132 increased the levels of SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and blocked their hypoxia-induced degradation (Figure 2C), confirming this degradation occurs via the proteasome.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2C

claim: MG132 blocked hypoxia-induced degradation of SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5.
source: Proteasomal inhibition using MG132 increased the levels of SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and blocked their hypoxia-induced degradation (Figure 2C), confirming this degradation occurs via the proteasome.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Hypoxia-induced degradation of SM occurs via the proteasome.
source: Proteasomal inhibition using MG132 increased the levels of SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and blocked their hypoxia-induced degradation (Figure 2C), confirming this degradation occurs via the proteasome.
evidence: Concluded from the MG132 inhibition experiment

claim: Protein levels and hypoxia-induced accumulation of trunSM were ablated by MG132.
source: We also noted that protein levels and hypoxia-induced accumulation of trunSM were ablated by MG132 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D), consistent with this protein arising from partial proteasomal proteolysis of SM (Coates et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D and citation to Coates et al., 2021

claim: trunSM arises from partial proteasomal proteolysis of SM.
source: We also noted that protein levels and hypoxia-induced accumulation of trunSM were ablated by MG132 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D), consistent with this protein arising from partial proteasomal proteolysis of SM (Coates et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coates et al., 2021

claim: Autophagy does not play a role in SM degradation during hypoxia.
source: Although hypoxia can trigger autophagy (Bellot et al., 2009), this did not play a role in SM degradation as inhibition of lysosomal acidification using bafilomycin A1 had no additive effect with MG132 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and citation to Bellot et al., 2009

claim: Hypoxia can trigger autophagy.
source: Although hypoxia can trigger autophagy (Bellot et al., 2009), this did not play a role in SM degradation as inhibition of lysosomal acidification using bafilomycin A1 had no additive effect with MG132 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bellot et al., 2009

claim: The magnitude of hypoxic degradation of SM was blunted by disruption of Lys-82/90/100.
source: The magnitude of hypoxic degradation was blunted by disruption of Lys-82/90/100, a cluster of redundant ubiquitination sites previously found to promote truncation (Coates et al., 2021), but not by disruption of Lys-290 (Figure 2D; Hornbeck et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citations to Coates et al., 2021 and Hornbeck et al., 2015

claim: Lys-82/90/100 is a cluster of redundant ubiquitination sites previously found to promote truncation.
source: The magnitude of hypoxic degradation was blunted by disruption of Lys-82/90/100, a cluster of redundant ubiquitination sites previously found to promote truncation (Coates et al., 2021), but not by disruption of Lys-290 (Figure 2D; Hornbeck et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coates et al., 2021

claim: Disruption of Lys-290 did not affect the magnitude of hypoxic degradation of SM.
source: The magnitude of hypoxic degradation was blunted by disruption of Lys-82/90/100, a cluster of redundant ubiquitination sites previously found to promote truncation (Coates et al., 2021), but not by disruption of Lys-290 (Figure 2D; Hornbeck et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Hornbeck et al., 2015

claim: Non-canonical cysteine, serine and threonine ubiquitination sites (SM-N100 C/S/T) are required for cholesterol-induced degradation of SM.
source: Non-canonical cysteine, serine and threonine ubiquitination sites required for the cholesterol-induced degradation of SM (SM-N100 C/S/T) (Chua et al., 2019) also contributed to hypoxia-induced degradation, suggesting multiple ubiquitin signals are involved.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chua et al., 2019

claim: Non-canonical cysteine, serine and threonine ubiquitination sites (SM-N100 C/S/T) contributed to hypoxia-induced degradation of SM.
source: Non-canonical cysteine, serine and threonine ubiquitination sites required for the cholesterol-induced degradation of SM (SM-N100 C/S/T) (Chua et al., 2019) also contributed to hypoxia-induced degradation, suggesting multiple ubiquitin signals are involved.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations

claim: Multiple ubiquitin signals are involved in hypoxia-induced degradation of SM.
source: Non-canonical cysteine, serine and threonine ubiquitination sites required for the cholesterol-induced degradation of SM (SM-N100 C/S/T) (Chua et al., 2019) also contributed to hypoxia-induced degradation, suggesting multiple ubiquitin signals are involved.
evidence: Inferred from the contribution of multiple ubiquitination sites

claim: Mutation of Lys-82/90/100 reduced SM levels under normoxic conditions.
source: Contrary to the expectation that loss of ubiquitination would stabilize SM, the mutation of Lys-82/90/100 reduced SM levels under normoxic conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: The Lys-82/90/100 cluster may be specifically involved in hypoxia-induced, rather than basal, degradation of SM.
source: Therefore, this cluster of residues may be specifically involved in hypoxia-induced, rather than basal, degradation of SM.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutation reduces normoxic levels

claim: Proline hydroxylation is required for the ubiquitination and degradation of HIF1α under normoxic conditions.
source: This oxygen-dependent modification, catalyzed by prolyl hydroxylases, is required for the ubiquitination and degradation of HIF1α under normoxic conditions (Ivan et al., 2001), although there is conflicting evidence for the existence of substrates beyond the HIF proteins (Cockman et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ivan et al., 2001 and Cockman et al., 2019

claim: Treatment with prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors DMOG and FG-4592 had no effect on the basal levels of SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5.
source: Indeed, treatment with the prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors DMOG and FG-4592 had no effect on the basal levels nor hypoxia-induced degradation of SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5, despite stabilizing HIF1α (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Treatment with prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors DMOG and FG-4592 had no effect on hypoxia-induced degradation of SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5.
source: Indeed, treatment with the prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors DMOG and FG-4592 had no effect on the basal levels nor hypoxia-induced degradation of SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5, despite stabilizing HIF1α (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: DMOG and FG-4592 stabilized HIF1α.
source: Indeed, treatment with the prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors DMOG and FG-4592 had no effect on the basal levels nor hypoxia-induced degradation of SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5, despite stabilizing HIF1α (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: SM and SM-N100 are targeted for proteasomal degradation by the E3 ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6.
source: SM and SM-N100 are targeted for proteasomal degradation by the E3 ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6 (Foresti et al., 2013; Zelcer et al., 2014); therefore, we tested if increased MARCHF6 activity could account for the hypoxia-induced degradation of SM.
evidence: Supported by citations to Foresti et al., 2013 and Zelcer et al., 2014

claim: Depletion of MARCHF6 dramatically increased SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5 levels.
source: SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5 levels were dramatically increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and the hypoxic decline in SM levels was blocked (Figure 3A), supporting the involvement of MARCHF6 in hypoxia-induced degradation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Depletion of MARCHF6 blocked the hypoxic decline in SM levels.
source: SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5 levels were dramatically increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and the hypoxic decline in SM levels was blocked (Figure 3A), supporting the involvement of MARCHF6 in hypoxia-induced degradation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: MARCHF6 is involved in hypoxia-induced degradation of SM.
source: SM and SM-N100-GFP-V5 levels were dramatically increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and the hypoxic decline in SM levels was blocked (Figure 3A), supporting the involvement of MARCHF6 in hypoxia-induced degradation.
evidence: Inferred from the MARCHF6 knockdown experiment results

claim: The basal levels of trunSM were reduced by MARCHF6 knockdown.
source: The basal levels and hypoxic accumulation of trunSM were also reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C), consistent with MARCHF6 contributing to the proteasomal targeting, and therefore partial degradation, of SM (Coates et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C and citation to Coates et al., 2021

claim: Hypoxic accumulation of trunSM was reduced by MARCHF6 knockdown.
source: The basal levels and hypoxic accumulation of trunSM were also reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C), consistent with MARCHF6 contributing to the proteasomal targeting, and therefore partial degradation, of SM (Coates et al., 2021).
